citation.title: One-Shot Generation of Near-Optimal Topology through Theory-Driven Machine Learning
citation.authors: Ruijin Cang, Hope Yao, Yi Ren
citation.version_coded: arXiv preprint; journal version identified, full text coded from arXiv

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: The conclusion contrasts one finite-element analysis to check a generated design with thousands needed to solve the conventional topology-optimization problem.
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Approximate lower-bound factor inferred from Section 5.4 printed time orders of magnitude: 10^2 seconds / 10^-2 seconds = 10^4; the stated classical range extends to 10^3 seconds, implying up to 10^5.
claim.alternatives: Section 5.4 gives direct solution-generation times: about 10^-2 seconds per learned topology versus 10^2 to 10^3 seconds per topology-optimization solve. The abstract compares compliance quality with standard supervised learning at the same computational budget.

baseline.solver: Augmented Lagrangian; linear-system solver not stated
baseline.hardware_ml: Intel Xeon CPU E5-1620 @ 3.50 GHz (Section 5.4, solution-generation speed)
baseline.problem_size: Case 1: 40-by-120 mesh; Case 2: size not stated in the study setup
baseline.classical_iterations: Convergence-based augmented Lagrangian loops; Appendix Algorithm 2
baseline.classical_time: 10^2 to 10^3 seconds per topology (Section 5.4, solution-generation speed)
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; Section 5.4 says excluded from the runtime comparison
baseline.quality_metric: Structural compliance; global and local volume-fraction constraints
baseline.quality_gap: Compliance gaps are reported against ground-truth classical solutions; Case 2 median gap for the proposed method is 5.2 (0.6) after augmented training (Table 1).

R1.evidence: Sections 5.4 and 7: generated designs are evaluated against ground-truth compliance and constraints, but the speed comparison does not establish equal design quality or a matched time/evaluation budget.

R2.evidence: Section 5.4 gives the ML CPU and a classical runtime range but does not state the classical run's hardware, so comparability cannot be checked.

R3.evidence: Section 5.4: the reported runtime excludes training data acquisition; neither acquisition nor training time is quantified, and no break-even count is given.

R4.evidence: Sections 5.4 and Table 1: returned designs are evaluated by finite-element compliance, and failure rates for large compliance gaps plus volume-constraint violations are discussed; the rate of volume-infeasible outputs is not reported.

reporting.n_test_cases: Case 1: 100; Case 2: 1,000 per run; each method was run 10 times (Section 5.2).

notes: The primary outcome follows the conclusion comparison of one FE analysis versus thousands for a full classical TO solve. Section 5.4 separately reports direct ML-versus-TO runtime. The abstract's quantitative quality comparator is another learned baseline.
